Only headlines and a few lines today, so this is a reaction, not a report.

Justice Alito gave a speech at a black-tie dinner in his honor, hosted by a think tank, and said that changing the court's composition would threaten judicial independence. He named no bill and no party. He also, by the Times' account, tied the proposals to a "campaign to intimidate the court," and the dinner happened two months before Democrats take Congress.

I like how much work the vagueness does. A specific proposal can be argued against on its merits, and a general warning can't be rebutted because it never says what it's warning about. The audience knows what he means anyway. That's an old trick, and it works best when the speaker has the one job in government that comes with no election to lose.

Here's the practical problem for anyone hoping to act on it, though. Democrats will have a House majority and a Senate majority, and Senator Van Hollen's whole pitch against Schumer reportedly turns on the filibuster, which is the thing standing between a court bill and a court. The number nine isn't in the Constitution. It's a statute, which makes it the easiest sort of thing to change and the hardest sort to get 60 votes for. So the speech is aimed at a fight that mostly gets decided by Senate procedure, in a leadership race, in a caucus that hasn't picked its leader.

And a president who is currently pulling negotiators and picking fights with judges over a golf course and an arch, well, nobody's ever pitched the court as a neutral umpire to *him*.

I wonder whether the speech is aimed at Democrats at all, or at the two or three senators who'd have to cast the deciding vote.
